implementation_notes: Ruby's native error channel is raise/rescue, so the Result contract arrives as a library: dry-monads provides Success(value) and Failure(error) under Dry::Monads[:result], with bind composing steps that may fail, fmap mapping the success value, value_or as the safe exit and value! as the deliberate unwrap that raises on a Failure; bind takes a block, so a step chain reads as ordinary Ruby (the docs' AssociateUser example nests bind and fmap exactly like a railway). The mixin is the canonical form and the reason this file recommends a library rather than hand-rolled objects, while raise/rescue stays the mainstream Ruby convention for exceptional paths. It pays off in service objects whose callers branch on structured failures and in batch flows.
code_sketch:
require 'dry/monads'

class AssociateUser
  include Dry::Monads[:result]

  def call(user_id:, address_id:)
    find_user(user_id).bind do |user|
      find_address(address_id).fmap do |address|
        user.update(address_id: address.id)
      end
    end
  end
end
pitfalls: Success/Failure are ordinary objects, so a caller who ignores the return value loses the failure silently; make the last result the method's return value and consume it at the boundary.
value! raises on Failure, reintroducing exceptions on the failure path; prefer value_or or the bind/fmap end block.
Including Dry::Monads[:result] injects the constructors into every object in the class, so fully qualified constants avoid leaking Success/Failure into unrelated code.

variants.name: hand-rolled Success/Failure with case/in
variants.implementation_notes: Without a dependency the same contract is two small value objects - Success(value) and Failure(error) - each with a bind/and_then that returns self or the other case, consumed by case/in pattern matching (stable since Ruby 3.0): case r in Success(value) ...; in Failure(error) ... end raises NoMatchingPatternError when no branch matches, which is the closest Ruby gets to a checked match. It avoids the gem and keeps failures as domain objects; the cost is that every helper (map, bind, value_or, an accumulation combinator) is yours to write and test, and raise/rescue remains the idiomatic channel for everything else.
variants.idiom_name: Success/Failure value objects consumed by case/in
variants.code_sketch:
Success = Data.define(:value)
Failure = Data.define(:error)

def parse_port(text)
  port = Integer(text, exception: false)
  return Failure.new(:not_a_number) if port.nil?
  0 < port && port < 65_536 ? Success.new(port) : Failure.new(:out_of_range)
end

case parse_port(raw)
in Success(value) then start(value)
in Failure(error) then log.error("invalid port: #{error}")
end
pitfalls: Data.define (Ruby 3.2) gives value equality cheaply; on 3.0/3.1 plain classes are required, and a Struct is mutable unless frozen.
case/in without else raises NoMatchingPatternError, which is the exhaustiveness a two-case value wants - but a value outside the two cases crashes the consumer instead of degrading.
